title: The hand that points to the foot
hookLine: one arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk and points at a lifted foot: why Hindus bow at the feet
carry: his lifted foot is grace; refuge is at his feet
tomorrow: who is the little figure under Shiva's foot?
last: THE BEGINNING IN ONE HAND, THE ENDING IN THE OTHER.

lines: A GUIDE WHO POINTS: THAT WAY.
ONE LOWER HAND: DO NOT FEAR.
THE OTHER POINTS AT THE FOOT.
cards: A guide at a busy train station doesn't take your suitcase or drag you to the platform. She lifts an arm and points: that way. Then she lets you walk.
Nataraja has a hand like that. Of his two lower hands, one is raised palm out, the do-not-fear gesture from the mudras. The other is the one to watch today.
It swings across his chest and hangs loose, and the fingers point down and across the body, at his raised foot.

teach.b: That arm has a name in the language of dance: gaja hasta, the elephant hand, because it hangs across the body the way an elephant's trunk swings. Notice what the hand doesn't do.
It doesn't hold anything, or grab, or push. It points, at the lifted foot. One foot is planted, pressing down; what's under it comes tomorrow.
The other foot is lifted clear of the ground.
In the usual reading, the planted foot presses down and holds, and the lifted foot is grace: release, the way out. Here is grace, says the hand. Look there.
And that's the teaching behind a gesture you'll see in any Hindu family.

teach.h: WHY HINDUS BOW AT THE FEET.
teach.b: The feet of the divine are where grace is, so they're where you bow. In temples, flowers are laid at the god's feet. In devotional poetry, taking refuge at the Lord's feet means surrender, trust, coming home.

And because parents, elders and teachers are honored as people that blessing flows through, children bend and touch their feet, and get a hand on the head in return. The Tamil poet-saint Appar sang of this foot.
In paraphrase: if you could see the arched brow, the smile, the matted hair and the lifted golden foot of the dancer, being born a human would be worth it.
So when a kid touches a grandmother's feet before an exam, that's the pointing hand, at home: grace is there; bow there. The hand doesn't drag you. It points, and leaves the walking to you.

how: Tamil hymns to Nataraja praise the lifted foot, which the lower hand points to; in worship, flowers are laid at the god's feet, and children touch the feet of parents, elders and teachers as a sign of respect and to receive their blessing.

o: a dancer's hand that grabs hold of a fallen demon
a hand gesture that means stop, used by temple guards
Shiva the dancer, here the hand that points to his lifted foot

games.q: hand and foot — tap the pairs.
p: Tamil poet-saint who sang of the foot

s: touching an elder's feet is just old-fashioned manners
it's the same bow as in the temple: the feet are where grace is honored, and the elder blesses you back.
the elephant hand is named for the way it swings like a trunk
gaja hasta: gaja, elephant; hasta, hand.
Appar sang that seeing the dancer's lifted foot would make human birth worth it
a reason to be glad to be in the world, not a ticket out of it.

games.q: your little cousin arrives at nani's and asks why she has to touch nani's feet. what do you tell her?
o: it's just manners, like shaking hands.
the feet are where grace is honored. Hindus bow at god's feet, and at an elder's, and the elder blesses you back.
it's to check her shoes are off.
games.why: Nataraja's hand points to his lifted foot for the same reason: the feet are where grace is, and where you bow.

practice: If an elder is near you today, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, you might bend and touch their feet, or bow to them in your heart.
Then rest your left arm loosely across your lap, fingers pointing down, and follow its line to your feet. Feel one foot planted, let the other feel light, and breathe there.
If you pray, bring your thoughts to the feet of Shiva, or of God.

wordCard.voice: Nataraja, the king of dancers. Today, the gaja hasta, the elephant hand that swings across the body and points to the lifted foot: grace, and the place to bow.

orig.note: Sanskrit: gaja hasta, from gaja (elephant) and hasta (hand): the arm that swings across Nataraja's body like a trunk.

carryVoice: Your line: his lifted foot is grace; refuge is at his feet. That's why Hindus bow there. Back tomorrow, same hill.
